title: Our Mutual Friend: A Literary Discussion

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked — a close reading of Charles Dickens's last completed novel, and arguably his strangest, most ambitious work.
Our Mutual Friend is a novel obsessed with money — where it comes from, what it does to people, and what people will do to get it.
Its opening image is a man dredging corpses from the Thames for profit.
Its closing vision is of a society that has monetised everything — goodness, love, death, and dust.
Over the course of this series, we'll work through the novel together — its characters, its language, its extraordinary atmosphere.
And I'm delighted to have three remarkable companions for the journey.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don whose career has been devoted to reading great novels as moral dramas — stories of character tested by circumstance.
He is, shall we say, not easily impressed by ideological readings — and that makes him a bracing voice in any literary conversation.
Professor James Blackstone brings legal and social history to bear on the novel's institutions — the law, poverty, the parish, the river trade.
He knows what it actually meant to be poor in Dickens's London, and he will not let us forget it.

And Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads novels as anatomies of class power — every character, every institution, every turn of plot seen as evidence of how a society organised itself around money and exclusion.
He will argue, with considerable force, that Dickens understood the system he was depicting better than he himself knew.
Gentlemen — welcome, all three of you.
Let's begin where the novel begins — with atmosphere.
Our Mutual Friend is saturated in a very particular mood — dark, gothic, tender, and satirical by turns.
James, I'd like to start with you — because the passages you've been looking at seem to me to capture the full range of this novel's atmosphere in miniature.
Thank you — and yes, that's exactly right.
What strikes me most about this novel is how completely Dickens refuses to let any single emotional register dominate.
Take Jenny Wren — the dolls' dressmaker — one of the novel's most peculiar and moving creations.
She lives in chronic pain, she supports a drunken father she calls her bad child, and yet she carries within her this extraordinary inner world.
There is a passage where she describes the visions that came to her in childhood — and it's unlike anything else in the novel.
She describes children in white descending in long bright rows, calling out to her.
"Who is this in pain! Who is this in pain!" When I told them who it was, they answered, "Come and play with us!"
Now — from a social historian's perspective — that is a child who has been so thoroughly excluded from ordinary childhood that she cannot even imagine playing.
Her only comfort is a visionary life — which is itself a measure of how little the real world offers her.
I'd grant you the social dimension, James, but I think that reading, if pursued too far, risks flattening something genuinely mysterious.
What Dickens is doing with Jenny Wren is something closer to what Johnson called the 'grandeur of generality.'
She stands for a kind of grace that suffering, when it doesn't destroy, can paradoxically produce.
Notice what she says about her birds and flowers — 'I dare say my birds sing better than other birds, and my flowers smell better than other flowers.'
That is not the language of deprivation demanding remedy.
That is the language of the imagination asserting its sovereignty over circumstance — which is, I would argue, the deepest thing this novel believes in.
Edmund, I admire the reading — genuinely — but I want to push on the word 'paradoxically.'
Because we should be clear about what Dickens is actually describing in that passage.
Jenny was chilled, anxious, ragged, beaten — those are Dickens's own words — and she 'never played.'
The imagination she develops is not a gift — it's a survival mechanism produced by conditions that should never have existed.
The vision is beautiful. The conditions that necessitated it are an indictment.
And Dickens — to his credit — doesn't let us forget either of those two things simultaneously.
Daniel is right, and I think the novel's atmosphere performs exactly that double movement throughout.
Consider the passage where Bradley Headstone creeps up the staircase outside Eugene Wrayburn's chambers in the dark.
Dickens describes his head as floating up the staircase — which is already deeply unsettling — and then he simply withdraws, leaving only a warning.

"If Lightwood could have seen the face which kept him awake, staring and listening in the darkness outside the door as he spoke of it, he might have been less disposed to sleep, through the remainder of the night."
What is remarkable there is the restraint.
Dickens does not describe the face. He describes the hypothetical terror of seeing it.
That is gothic technique at its most precise — and it speaks to something very deliberate about how this novel constructs menace.
The Headstone passages are among the most extraordinary in the whole novel, I think.
Here is a man of genuine merit — self-educated, professionally respectable — destroyed by a passion he cannot govern.
That is a moral drama of the oldest kind — weakness of will meeting force of circumstance — and it has nothing to do with class per se.
The haggard head floating up that dark staircase is the image of a mind that has already, in the truest sense, vacated its own moral habitation.
I won't entirely disagree with Edmund on Headstone — the moral psychology is brilliantly rendered.
But we should notice that Bradley Headstone's violence is not random — it is directed upward, at the class that effortlessly possesses what he has had to claw for.
And Dickens reserves some of his most piercing satirical intelligence for the other end of the spectrum — for Wegg, the petty schemer, whose spite he anatomises with wonderful cold comedy.
"The yard or two of smile on the part of the alligator might have been invested with the meaning, 'All about this was quite familiar knowledge down in the depths of the slime, ages ago.'"
The alligator has seen it all before.
Envy, betrayal, the transformation of a benefactor into an enemy — these are not social pathologies peculiar to Victorian England.
They are the slime at the bottom of every era's river, and Dickens knows it.
There's one more passage I want to bring in, because it captures something the novel does that I find almost unbearably powerful.
John Harmon, drugged and thrown into the Thames, describes the moment consciousness returns to him while he is drowning.
After — and I quote directly — 'a downward slide through something like a tube, and then a great noise and a sparkling and crackling as of fires' — consciousness speaks to him.
"This is John Harmon drowning! John Harmon, struggle for your life. John Harmon, call on Heaven and save yourself!"
The self speaking to the self in extremis — naming itself so it will not dissolve.
That is identity itself under threat — and in a novel built on questions of who people really are, it's the most concentrated image of the whole book's central anxiety.
Pain, menace, satire, and a man naming himself so he won't drown — all in a handful of passages.
That is the range of Our Mutual Friend, and that is what we'll be exploring in the weeks ahead.
In our next segment, we turn to the novel's great central obsession — money, inheritance, and the dust heaps that started it all.

segments.title: Bella's Reckoning: From Mercenary to Moral

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
Today we are diving into one of the novel's most quietly astonishing achievements: the transformation of Bella Wilfer.
Bella begins the novel as a self-declared mercenary — furious that the man she was to inherit died before she could meet him, let alone love him.
And yet she ends it as one of Dickens's most warmly realised moral portraits.
To untangle how that happens — and whether it fully convinces — we have three remarkable guides with us today.
Sir Edmund Leigh brings the classical literary instinct — character tested by circumstance, the moral imagination at the heart of great fiction.
Professor James Blackstone situates the novel's institutions and social machinery in the hard facts of Victorian life.
And Dr. Daniel Rosen reads the novel as an anatomy of class power — asking whose interests are served by any apparent redemption.
Edmund, let us begin with you — because I think the arc Bella travels is precisely the kind of individual moral drama you find most compelling in fiction.
Thank you — and yes, Bella is, to my mind, the finest argument in this novel for what fiction can do that sociology simply cannot.
She begins with something quite honest about herself, which is rare.
She knows she is mercenary and says so — and that self-knowledge, however unflattering, is the seed of everything that follows.
But to understand what she is being tested against, we should look at the world the novel sets around her.
Consider Eugene Wrayburn — a man who has been disposed of by his father before he was even born, in a manner of speaking.
Dickens gives us Eugene describing his family with that extraordinary cool wit of his.
"When my second brother was going to be born by-and-by, 'this,' says M. R. F., 'is a little pillar of the church.' Was born, and became a pillar of the church; a very shaky one."
A very shaky one — delivered with that perfect Dickensian deadpan.
The point being: in this novel, fathers pre-assign destinies.
Old Harmon attempted to assign Bella a husband from beyond the grave.
What is remarkable about Bella is that she escapes that assignation — not by rejecting it violently, but by growing into something the dead hand never anticipated: genuine moral character.
Edmund is right that Bella escapes the paternal script — but I want to press on what that script actually was in legal and social terms.
Old Harmon's will is not a Gothic eccentricity — it is a perfectly coherent exercise of testamentary power as Victorian law conceived it.
A man could attach conditions to an inheritance that bound living people to arrangements they had no voice in making.
And young John Harmon — the supposed heir — internalises this profoundly.
His scheme to observe Bella incognito is described in remarkably clinical terms.
"The plot was made out of our getting common sailors' dresses, and throwing ourselves in Bella Wilfer's neighbourhood, and trying to put ourselves in her way."
Now, one might read that as romantic ingenuity — and it is, up to a point.
But it is also a wealthy man conducting a covert audit of a woman's character before deciding whether to claim her.
The power differential is baked into the very structure of the courtship.
James has put his finger on something essential, and I want to push it further.
When John Harmon explains why he chose to remain dead for a time, the language he uses is revealing.
"The dread of our being forced on one another, and perpetuating the fate that seemed to have fallen on my father's riches — the fate that they should lead to nothing but evil."
He calls it moral timidity dating from his childhood — but what is the actual operation here?
A man with enormous inherited wealth decides to test a woman who has none.
The novel frames this as proving Bella — as if her worth must be verified before the wealth descends.
That structure — wealth as arbiter, woman as candidate — is not incidental to the novel's ideology.
It is its deepest assumption, operating even inside its most sympathetic romance.
Daniel's reading is coherent, and I won't pretend the power asymmetry isn't there.
But I think it misses the emotional weight of what Dickens is actually doing with Bella's interiority.
The transformation is not imposed on her from outside — it wells up from within.
And we see it reflected — obliquely, beautifully — in the scene at Eugene and Lizzie's bedside marriage.
Bella is present at that ceremony, and Dickens tells us she wept — thinking of her own sunny little wedding.
And then comes the image that seems to me to define what love means in this novel.

"When the two plighted their troth, she laid her hand on his and kept it there. When the ceremony was done, and all the rest departed from the room, she drew her arm under his head, and laid her own head down upon the pillow by his side."
Kept it there — those three words carry the whole moral weight of the novel's idea of fidelity.
And Bella, watching that, has already become a woman capable of recognising it.
That scene is extraordinary — and it earns its power precisely because Dickens insists on the physical reality of Eugene's condition.
As the bridegroom could not move his hand, they touched his fingers with the ring — and so put it on the bride.
The legal and ceremonial form is being honoured under conditions it was never designed for.
Which is, in miniature, what Dickens does throughout the whole novel: he subjects inherited forms to the pressure of actual human feeling.
And the contrast with Bradley Headstone is instructive here.
Bradley is also consumed — but by something that forecloses all connection rather than enabling it.
Bradley Headstone is the novel's most devastating portrait of what the class system does to the human person from the inside.
He is a self-made man in the Victorian sense — dragged up by education from absolute poverty, trained into respectability.
And what that process has produced is a man whose inner life is a furnace with no outlet.
Look at how Dickens renders his final vigil before the fire.

"Rigid before the fire, as if it were a charmed flame that was turning him old, he sat, with the dark lines deepening in his face, its stare becoming more and more haggard, its surface turning whiter and whiter as if it were being overspread with ashes, and the very texture and colour of his hair degenerating."
Overspread with ashes — he is being cremated from within.
This is what the system produces when it gives a man just enough education to feel his own exclusion acutely, but no structural means of escape.
Bella's transformation is real — I don't dispute that — but it is available to her precisely because she is positioned differently in the social order than Bradley is.
She can grow. He can only burn.
That is forcefully put — and the contrast does illuminate something Dickens almost certainly intended.
Though I would argue that Bradley's tragedy is not merely sociological — it is fundamentally a failure of the moral will.
He chooses violence at every turning point where he might have chosen otherwise.
What makes Bella's arc instructive by contrast is not her social position but her receptivity — her willingness to be changed by love and by honesty.
One need not share every one of Dickens's assumptions about class to find that genuinely moving.
And Dickens does not let the comedy go entirely, even here — there is Sloppy in his magnificent new suit, heroically defeating the tailor's best efforts.
He is described as having stood before the assembled company as — Dickens puts it memorably —
"a perfect Argus in the way of buttons: shining and winking and gleaming and twinkling out of a hundred of those eyes of bright metal, at the dazzled spectators."
The comedy holds its place alongside the tragedy — and that tonal range is, to my mind, what makes this novel exceptional rather than merely serious.
What a compass the novel holds — from Bradley's annihilating despair to Sloppy's mutinous buttons.
And at the centre of it all, Bella — who begins by knowing her own worst self and ends by outgrowing it.
In our next segment, we will look more closely at the novel's treatment of money itself — what it does to those who have it, those who want it, and those it simply passes over entirely.

segments.title: The Machinery of Class: Boffin's Rise and the Social Order

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the programme that takes Dickens's great novel of money, mud, and moral reckoning and turns it over in the light.
I'm your host, and today we are deep inside what I want to call the machinery of class — the gears and levers by which wealth confers status, and status invites predation.
With me are three guests who bring very different instruments to this examination.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who reads the novel as a story of individual character tested by circumstance — goodness, weakness, and the will to choose.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who brings the real institutions to bear — what the law actually meant, what poverty actually was.
And Dr Daniel Rosen reads the novel as an anatomy of class power — every act of charity, every inheritance, every scheme, as a mechanism for protecting the rich.
We begin with the moment that sets everything in motion: the death of John Harmon, and what his money does to the world around it.
What strikes me first about the inquest passages is how completely the novel frames death as a financial event.
John Harmon is barely cold before the public interest attaches not to who he was but to what he carried.
Dickens is precise about the sum — and deliberately so.

The testimony establishes that the deceased Mr John Harmon did bring over, in a hand-valise with which he did disembark, the sum realized by the forced sale of his little landed property, and that the sum exceeded, in ready money, seven hundred pounds.
Seven hundred pounds, in a hand-valise.
That image — portable, concentrated, vulnerable — is the novel's inaugural symbol of what money is and what it does to people who know it exists nearby.
And then society immediately converts the dead man's story into dinner-table property.
Daniel is right that Dickens is precise about the money — but I want to resist the reduction of the scene to economics alone.
What Dickens is actually anatomising here is a failure of moral imagination on the part of society at large.
Veneering, Twemlow, Podsnap — they all relate the circumstances irreconcilably with one another, and contradicted themselves.
That comic multiplication of inaccuracies is not merely a class satire — it is a portrait of minds incapable of attending to what actually happened to a human being.
The money matters to Dickens, yes — but what he is really watching is the moral deformation that money produces in those who merely hear of it.
Both of those readings are illuminating, but I want to ground us for a moment in what an inquest actually was in Dickens's England.
The coroner's inquest was one of the few legal proceedings where the bodies of the poor — and the money of anyone — became public record.

Jesse Hexam's celebrated career of retrieving corpses from the Thames is rewarded with eighteen postage stamps and five letters to the Times — and Dickens cannot resist noting that the admirer signs himself 'A friend to Burial,' perhaps an undertaker.
That parenthetical is the whole novel in miniature — the economy of death, and the self-interest that dresses itself as sentiment.
The economy of death — that phrase takes us directly to what happens when the Harmon fortune lands on Nicodemus Boffin.
Because within days of the Golden Dustman's elevation, the machinery of charitable extraction swings into motion — and it is one of the most brilliantly savage passages in the novel.
The Secretary's catalogue of letters is a genuine sociological document, and I use that word without irony.

In mid-Victorian England, charitable institutions proliferated at a rate that made systematic oversight impossible — and that vacuum was filled by exactly the kind of aristocratic letterhead Dickens lampoons here.
The Duke of Linseed's letter is the centrepiece — and Dickens sets it up with exquisite precision.
Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet.
Every adjective is doing work — large, fat, private, double — the physical bulk of aristocratic entitlement, before a word of the contents is read.
And the postscript — the Steward's fee is limited to three Guineas — is, as Dickens notes, 'friendly and thoughtful,' lithographed by the hundred.
What James is describing is the circulatory system of class extraction — charity as the polite name for a levy imposed on new money by established power.
But I want to move from the institutional beggars to the individual ones, because that is where Dickens's anger becomes truly extraordinary.
He notes that these correspondents all enclose documents — and then he delivers what I think is one of his most perfectly turned comparisons.
They call their scraps documents; but they are, as to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf.
Minced veal to a calf — the reduction of lived desperation to bureaucratic fiction, and Dickens sees both sides of that reduction with absolute clarity.
These people are genuinely ruined — he says so explicitly — and their ruin has forced them into a performance of ruin that is somehow even more degrading than the ruin itself.
I find myself in the unusual position of agreeing with Daniel entirely on the quality of the writing — and differing only on its ultimate significance.
The parade of individual beggars — the inspired, the suggestively-befriended, the nobly independent, the ones who will be cold in death at a quarter to one — this is not a taxonomy of class.
It is a catalogue of the varieties of moral self-deception available to the desperate.
Dickens is simultaneously compassionate and merciless — and that combination is a mark of great moral imagination, not social programme.
The compassion and the mercilessness held in tension — that seems to me the heart of what makes these passages so uncomfortable.
And that tension intensifies enormously when we turn to what Silas Wegg and Mr Venus are doing in the shadows — because they represent a very different kind of predation on Boffin's fortune.
Wegg is one of Dickens's most purely comic villains, and I think it is a mistake to read him as anything more elevated than that.
He is a man of magnificent self-regard and negligible capacity — and his reading of the will confirms this with wonderful economy.
The elder Harmon's final verdict on human connection is delivered through Wegg in just one sentence — and it is quite devastating.

Inasmuch as he has never made friends, and has ever had a rebellious family, he, John Harmon, gives to Nicodemus Boffin the Little Mound, which is quite enough for him, and gives the whole rest and residue of his property to the Crown.
'Quite enough for him' — three words of patrician contempt from beyond the grave, and Wegg reads them without the faintest awareness of what they imply.
The legal dimension here is genuinely interesting — and rather dark.
A testator in Victorian England could leave the residue of his estate to the Crown — and this was not, in practice, mere eccentricity.
It was a deliberate act of disinheritance so absolute that even the state's indifference was preferable to rewarding one's family.
The elder Harmon has used the law as a final instrument of punishment — and what Wegg is now trying to do is use that same instrument as an instrument of extortion.
And that continuity is precisely what makes Wegg's scheme so structurally revealing.
Wegg is not an aberration — he is a mirror of the system.
His plan is nothing more than the charity-extraction racket of the Duke of Linseed, made explicit and honest about its coercive nature.
And Dickens gives Wegg language that almost parodies the language of legitimate property relations — listen to this.

He considered it plain that such price was stateable in a single expressive word, and that the word was, 'Halves!' — and he should be kept in a state of abject moral bondage and slavery until the time when they should see fit to permit him to purchase his freedom at the price of half his possessions.
'Abject moral bondage and slavery' — Wegg reaches instinctively for the vocabulary of unfreedom, because at bottom that is what property-based power has always required.
The novel knows this even when its characters do not.
I'll concede the phrase is extraordinary — 'abject moral bondage and slavery' emerging from the mouth of a man who can barely read without stumbling.
But the comedy is the point.
Wegg's grandiosity is the grandiosity of a man who has mistaken his own cupidity for principle — and Dickens exposes that confusion with affectionate contempt.
He is not a symptom of capitalism — he is a study in the universal human capacity to dress self-interest in the language of justice.
The language of justice worn over self-interest — and yet the novel also insists on showing us what genuine degradation looks like, stripped of all such language.

Before we close this segment, I want to ask Daniel about a passage assigned to him that operates in a completely different register — Jenny Wren's father, and Eugene Wrayburn, and a single brief moment of embodied ruin.
This passage almost defies the kind of reading I normally do — because it is so purely physical, so concentrated in the body.
Dickens gives us a portrait of a man whose poverty has become somatic — it has moved into his joints, into the involuntary failure of his limbs.
The sentence that opens the passage is remarkable — hear it.
The miserable man, feebly rubbing the back of his faltering hands downward from the wrists, shuffled on to his post of disgrace.
'Post of disgrace' — as though degradation has a designated station, a fixed point in the household geography where the ruined man is required to stand.
And Eugene notices him only by instinctively falling away from the disagreeable contact — the casual reflex of a gentleman encountering human wreckage.
The social order does not need Wegg's schemes to enforce itself — it is reproduced in a cigar lit and a departure made without a second glance.
That observation is genuinely penetrating, and I will not quarrel with it.
What I would add is that the passage is also a study in what habitual vice does to a person — this man has drunk himself into a condition where even voluntary action has become uncertain.
Dickens is tracking the moral and the physical simultaneously — and refusing to separate them.
The question I always want to ask about these passages is what the alternative was — what else could a man in his position have done.

In the 1860s, a man who could no longer work reliably had no recourse outside family or the workhouse — and Dickens is showing us the domestic version of the workhouse, Jenny Wren as his keeper and his judge.
That 'post of disgrace' is not merely Jenny's invention — it is what the social order would assign him, if the social order noticed him at all.

The post of disgrace — and whether the social order assigns it, or the individual earns it, or both: that is a question this novel refuses to resolve cleanly, which is part of why we are still arguing about it.
In our next segment, we'll be following the river further — looking at what it means to live entirely outside the mechanisms of property and charity that we've been examining today.

segments.title: Harmon's Shadow: Identity, Plot, and Narrative Deception

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's great, sprawling, deeply strange final completed novel seriously — in every sense.

I'm your host, and today we're gathering to examine one of the novel's most elaborate pieces of machinery: the Harmon murder, the identity games it sets in motion, and the deceptions — narrative and moral — that flow from it.
With me today are three scholars who bring very different lenses to this extraordinary book.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don whose life's work has been reading novels as moral imaginative acts — stories about character under pressure, not social programmes.
Edmund brings an unfashionable but formidably argued case: that what makes Dickens great is his humanity, not his politics.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who knows what it actually meant, in the 1860s, to be poor, to work the river, and to exist at the mercy of institutions.
He is our indispensable corrective whenever the novel risks becoming merely picturesque.
And Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads every institution in a novel — the law, philanthropy, the inheritance system — as a mechanism of class power.
Daniel's argument is that the greatest novelists were more radical than they knew — and he brings the evidence to prove it.
Let's begin with the heart of today's segment: what the novel does with death, identity, and the story it tells before we know what story it's actually telling.
What strikes me, coming back to these early chapters, is the sheer audacity of Dickens's narrative construction.
We are asked to mourn a man we have barely met, on the basis of a body whose identity is in doubt from the first page.
And yet the moral gravity of the situation is entirely real — because Boffin makes it real.
His account of defending young John Harmon against his father's cruelty is, I think, one of the most quietly devastating passages in the novel.
He says, and I want to read this carefully —

'I have seen him, after Mrs Boffin has given him her mind respecting the claims of the nat'ral affections, catch off Mrs Boffin's bonnet — she wore, in general, a black straw, perched as a matter of convenience on the top of her head — and send it spinning across the yard.'
And then the sentence arrives at its destination: 'received flush on the temple. Which dropped her, Mr Lightwood. Dropped her.'
That repetition — 'Dropped her' — is not sentiment; it is testimony.
Boffin is a witness standing in the dock of memory, and he will not let the fact pass without its full weight.
Edmund is right that Boffin is bearing witness — and I think we need to take seriously what that witnessing costs, in social terms.
Boffin and Mrs Boffin are servants — bound labour, effectively — standing up to a patriarch who controls their entire economic existence.
Old Harmon had, in Boffin's own phrase, wrung as much work out of them as could be got in their best days, for as little money as could be paid to hurry on their worst.
That is a portrait of exploitation so precise it could serve as a legal brief.
And yet their moral character survives it — and the novel insists that it more than survives; it prevails against the very nature that sought to degrade it.
That is a remarkable claim for a novelist to make, and Dickens does not make it sentimentally.
James has put his finger on exactly the passage I wanted to return to — the narrator's great aphoristic statement about Good and Evil.
Dickens writes, and I find it impossible not to quote this directly —
'For, Evil often stops short at itself and dies with the doer of it; but Good, never.'
Dr. Johnson himself could not have said it more economically.
It is the novel's moral spine, stated baldly and without apology at the very point where the reader might be tempted to dismiss the Boffins as comic figures.
I don't want to quarrel with either of those readings — but I think we risk making the novel more comfortable than it is.
The narrator calls the Boffins 'ignorant and unpolished' — and that is Dickens's phrase, not Old Harmon's.
Even in the act of celebrating their goodness, the novel cannot quite release its grip on class condescension.
Their virtue is certified by a system that already owns them — that is the novel's structural problem, and it is there on the page.
And when we turn to the Riderhood accusation, that structural problem sharpens into something truly frightening.
Riderhood presents himself before the law and pronounces —

'I give information that the man that done the Harmon Murder is Gaffer Hexam, the man that found the body. The hand of Jesse Hexam, commonly called Gaffer on the river and along shore, is the hand that done that deed. His hand and no other.'
That triple repetition of 'hand' is not rhetoric — it is a man performing certainty he cannot possibly possess.
And the system accepts it. The law writes it down. That is what power does with an accusation when it comes from below — it uses it, and then it dispenses with the accuser.
Daniel has identified something historically precise there.
In the 1860s, an informant of Riderhood's class had almost no standing in law except as an instrument — rewarded for the accusation, discarded once it had served its purpose.
And the novel gives that irony its full due, because the accusation is false — and yet it destroys a man anyway.
Gaffer Hexam is found dead before the truth can be established. And Riderhood's response — 'Gaffer's done me. It's Gaffer!' — is purely about what the death means for his own position.
There is no grief, no guilt, no recognition that a human life has ended through his agency.
The river takes Gaffer; the novel records that fact with a kind of terrible neutrality.
I want to stay with that phrase — 'Gaffer's done me' — for a moment.
Because it is, in its way, a masterpiece of moral inversion.
Riderhood has accused an innocent man of murder. That man is now dead — found by the river, the very instrument of his trade.
And the response is to feel cheated. Not of justice. Of money.
Dickens does not editorialize. He does not need to. The sentence — 'It's Gaffer!' — carries its own verdict.
And yet the novel cannot quite stay in that dark place — it needs a counter-image, something to set against the river's cruelty and Riderhood's cupidity.
And it finds one in an extraordinary rooftop scene — Lizzie Hexam and Jenny Wren, reading together above the city.
The narrator describes it carefully —
'Lizzie Hexam and Jenny Wren. For whom, perhaps with some old instinct of his race, the gentle Jew had spread a carpet... they both pored over one book; both with attentive faces.'
Two women, excluded from every institution the novel has described, making their own small, fierce act of self-education.
That is the novel's radical image — not the inheritance, not the dust-heap, but two women poring over a book on a rooftop above all of it.
And Riah's role in that scene is worth noting — he has furnished the carpet, the books, the fruit.
He has created, on the rooftop of a city that would grind all three of them down, a small space of dignity and learning.
The novel notes 'a common basket of common fruit' — that repeated word, common, is doing real work.
It is common — ordinary, shared, unadorned — and it is enough. That is the novel's counter-argument to the dust-heap inheritance.
I find I cannot quarrel with either of you on this passage — and that itself is rather remarkable.
The chimney-stacks 'twirling their cowls and fluttering their smoke, rather as if they were bridling, and fanning themselves, and looking on in a state of airy surprise' — that is pure comic delight.
The city itself is astonished by what it sees. And so, I confess, am I.

What I take from this extraordinary circuit of passages is that Dickens has constructed a novel in which the question of identity — who is dead, who is guilty, who deserves the money — keeps dissolving every time we think we've answered it.
The Harmon murder, it turns out, is less a mystery to be solved than a prism through which the novel examines what society does to the bodies of the poor — in life, and in death.
Edmund, James, Daniel — thank you for this. We'll return, in our next segment, to the question of what the novel's great inheritance plot actually inherits — and what it buries.

segments.title: The Comic Mask: Humour as Social Instrument

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
We've been exploring the novel's darker registers — the river, the dust, the machinery of money.
But Dickens was also, and almost always, very funny — and the humour in this novel does serious work.
James Blackstone has been assigned some of the novel's most charged comic moments today.
James brings his historian's eye for institutions and their human costs — and his very dry sense of what's actually going on behind a laugh.
Edmund Leigh reads humour as Dickens at his most morally alert — character revealing itself under comic pressure.
And Daniel Rosen will want to ask — who is the joke on, and what does it cost them?
James, let's begin with Silas Wegg and the extraordinary mime he performs outside Boffin's keyhole.
That scene is one of the most unsettling comic moments in the entire novel, and I think it's worth sitting with precisely why.
Wegg is a one-legged ballad-monger who has spent the novel convincing himself he deserves a share of Boffin's fortune.
He has no legitimate claim whatsoever — but he's accumulated just enough knowledge to make himself dangerous.
And here is the image Dickens gives us for that power.
'Silas made no reply, but laboured with a will at turning an imaginary grindstone outside the keyhole, while Mr Boffin stooped at it within; he then laughed silently, and stumped home.'
An imaginary grindstone.
The instrument of power is purely theatrical — mimed, wordless — and yet Boffin stoops to it anyway.
That's a precise image for how blackmail actually works — and how class resentment can become its own grotesque performance.
James puts his finger on something important about the silent laugh at the end of that passage.
Wegg doesn't cackle. He laughs silently, then stumps home.
There is something deeply inward and cold about that — it speaks to a character entirely self-enclosed in his own malice.
And yet Dickens has made him physically comic — the stump, the literary pretensions, the preposterous ballads.
The comedy is not softening Wegg's villainy. It is exposing what villainy looks like when it has no dignity to lose.
I'd press a little further on that word 'performance,' because I think the class dimension here is doing precise work.
Wegg is enacting the only power available to someone in his position — the power of witnessed contempt.
He cannot own the wealth. He cannot litigate for it. He can mime a grindstone and make Boffin feel it.
What Dickens has captured is a very specific feature of extortion under conditions of radical inequality: the sheer economy of cruelty available to those with nothing else to trade.
The comedy doesn't soften that — it clarifies it, makes it legible in a way that straight drama couldn't quite manage.
There's a very different kind of comic energy when we turn to Jenny Wren and Fledgeby — because that one has a moral verdict built right into the laughter.
James, how do you read the pepper scene?
Jenny Wren — Miss Wren, the dolls' dressmaker — is one of the novel's most remarkable figures precisely because she operates entirely outside the usual channels of redress.
She cannot sue Fledgeby. She cannot report him. She has no institutional recourse of any kind.
What she has is pepper — and the moral reasoning she brings to applying it is, I think, scrupulously Dickensian.
'I think the young man's tricks and manners make a claim upon his friends for a little pepper?'
A claim. She uses the language of entitlement — precisely the language Fledgeby himself deploys to exploit others.
The comedy is the justice system in miniature — swift, proportionate, delivered with a silent laugh.
And note the silent laugh again — Dickens uses it twice, for Wegg and for Jenny Wren.
But these are two very different silences.
Wegg's silence is self-congratulatory, cold, essentially predatory.
Jenny Wren's is something else — it carries the controlled delight of someone who has found, at last, a proportionate response to an injustice they cannot otherwise remedy.
Dickens is using the same comic device to draw a moral distinction that is absolutely clear without ever being stated.
Daniel is right, and I'd add that Jenny Wren's comedy is always edged with something the novel doesn't let us forget.
She is in pain — chronic, unrelenting physical pain — and yet her wit is entirely unbroken.
That conjunction — suffering and comic intelligence held simultaneously — is what elevates her beyond caricature.
She is, in her way, a figure of genuine moral heroism — expressed through mischief rather than suffering meekly endured.
Let's turn to a very different kind of comic portrait — Twemlow, and the narrator's extraordinary tenderness toward him.
James, you've been assigned a passage about him that reads more like elegy than satire.
Yes, and the shift in register is deliberate and, I think, moving.
Twemlow is a figure of pure social comedy for much of the novel — a mild, bewildered little man used as a dinner-table credential by the Veneerings.
But the narrator pauses over him — really pauses — and what we get is this.
'Good childish creature! Condemned to a passage through the world by such narrow little dimly-lighted ways, and picking up so few specks or spots on the road!'
The comedy has dissolved entirely. What remains is pity — genuine, unsentimental pity.
His innocence, which has been the source of the joke throughout, is now understood as a kind of tragic confinement.
That exclamation — 'Good childish creature!' — is not ironic. It cannot be read as ironic.
The narrator is, for a moment, entirely without armour — expressing something very close to love for this slight, ineffectual man.
And that, I'd argue, is Dickens's greatest moral gift — the capacity to find, in the comic, the genuinely pitiable, and to honour it without condescension.
The narrow, dimly-lighted ways are not a metaphor for systems. They are Twemlow's actual life — and the narrator mourns them.
I won't quite let the metaphor go so easily, though.
Those narrow, dimly-lighted ways — what has produced them? Twemlow has been a social accessory his entire life, valued only for his connection to a lord.
His innocence is not simply a personal quality — it is a structural product of a class that kept him ornamental and excluded him from consequence.
The tenderness of the narrator is real — Edmund is absolutely right about that — but the tenderness is also an indictment.
That tension — between individual virtue and structural limitation — runs through our final passage as well: Mrs Sprodgkin and the Milveys.
James, this is a scene that Dickens frames as comic but then explicitly honours.
The Milveys are conscientious clergymen operating in a world that gives them very little with which to work.

Mrs Sprodgkin is their comic affliction — a parishioner of weaponised piety who appears precisely when least desired, demanding elucidation on questions like, as the narrator puts it, 'Who begat Whom, or some information concerning the Amorites.'
And her understanding of charitable gifts is — well, there is a particular grandeur to it.
'She regarded tea and sugar in the light of myrrh and frankincense, and considered bread and butter identical with locusts and wild honey.'
The comedy there is theological — she has elevated the mundane into the sacred to avoid gratitude.
But what interests me is the narrator's coda: he records all this 'to the honour of that good Christian pair.'
The comedy and the commendation coexist. That is a very precise moral operation.
What Dickens is doing there is distinguishing between the absurdity of the situation and the character of those who endure it.
Goodness, in this novel, is almost always practised in circumstances that would make a lesser novelist reach for tragedy.
Dickens gives us comedy instead — and in doing so, he suggests that genuine virtue doesn't require grand theatrical display.
They merge, the narrator says, 'the smallness of their work in its greatness.' That is a doctrine, quietly stated.
The Milveys are sympathetic, and I'll grant Edmund the warmth of this portrait.
But I want to bring in the Bella passage from this cluster, because it sharpens what Dickens thinks comedy and performance actually do.
Boffin's performance of avarice — his deliberate acting out of the miser — is the novel's most extended comic-moral experiment.
And when Bella finally decodes it, she articulates Boffin's logic with devastating clarity.

'This shallow creature would never work the truth out of her own weak soul, if she had a hundred years to do it in; but a glaring instance kept before her may open even her eyes and set her thinking.'
Comedy — performance, exaggeration — deployed as a pedagogy.
That is the novel's theory of its own humour, stated plainly. Dickens knew what he was doing with the comic mask.
A pedagogy — a glaring instance — that's a beautiful note to carry forward.
What Dickens makes us feel, laughing, is also what he needs us to think.
In our next segment, we'll be turning to the novel's formal and narrative structures — how Dickens controls time, perspective, and revelation.
Thank you, James, Edmund, Daniel — and thank you for listening.

segments.title: Dickens's Interwoven Worlds: Technique and Meaning

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the programme that takes Dickens's great last completed novel seriously — on its own terms, in its full complexity.
I'm your host, and today we're examining how Dickens weaves together individual character, memory, and the corrupting force of inherited wealth.
With me are three scholars who bring very different lenses to this extraordinary novel.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who reads Dickens as a moral imaginationist — interested above all in goodness tested by circumstance.
Professor James Blackstone brings the historian's eye — the real institutions, the actual law, the lived texture of Victorian poverty.
And Dr. Daniel Rosen reads the novel as an anatomy of class power — asking always who benefits and who pays.
Edmund, let's begin with you — because one of the passages before us today seems to go to the very heart of what you care about in fiction.
Boffin recounting young John Harmon at the fireside — a child of seven, alone, about to be sent away to a foreign school.
What does Dickens achieve in that passage?
What Dickens achieves there is, I think, one of the most quietly devastating pieces of retrospective pathos in the entire novel.
It arrives without warning, delivered in Boffin's rough, unschooled voice — and that roughness is precisely the point.
The tenderness is not literary. It is not cultivated. It is simply there, in the man.
The passage I keep returning to — and I think it bears reading aloud — is this.
"There was his little scanty travelling clothes upon him. There was his little scanty box outside in the shivering wind, which I was going to carry for him down to the steamboat."
"Mrs Boffin, then quite a young woman and pictur of a full-blown rose, stands him by her, kneels down at the fire, warms her two open hands, and falls to rubbing his cheeks."

"But seeing the tears come into the child's eyes, the tears come fast into her own, and she holds him round the neck, like as if she was protecting him, and cries to me, 'I'd give the wide wide world, I would, to run away with him!'"
That repetition — "wide wide world" — is not rhetorical flourish.
It is the sound of a feeling too large for ordinary language, spoken by a woman whose vocabulary is not large at all.
And that, to my mind, is Dickens's moral imagination at its finest — placing an enormous human truth inside the most unassuming vessel.
Edmund is absolutely right to dwell on the vessel, if I may put it that way.
What strikes me as a historian is the extraordinary specificity of the detail Dickens puts into Boffin's account.
The old man wouldn't hear of allowing a sixpence coach-money — that one detail tells you everything about old Harmon Senior's relationship to money and to this child.
In mid-Victorian England, sending a child of seven abroad unaccompanied to a foreign school was not merely cold — it was, in any meaningful sense, an act of deliberate cruelty.
The steamboat, the shivering wind, the scanty box — these are not romantic flourishes.
They are the material conditions of a particular kind of Victorian childhood deprivation, rendered with documentary precision.
I want to hold onto that word 'cruelty' for a moment, because I think Dickens is doing something more precise than sentiment here.
The scene is presented as exceptional — as Boffin and his wife feeling extraordinary compassion for this particular child.
But Dickens quietly shows us that their compassion changes nothing.
The boy is still sent away. Boffin still carries the box to the steamboat. The old man's command still holds.
And then there is this — the way the memory haunts Mrs Boffin.

"So of a night, when it was very cold, or when the wind roared, or the rain dripped heavy, she would wake sobbing, and call out in a fluster, 'Don't you see the poor child's face? O shelter the poor child!'"
The capacity to feel has been preserved in these two people — and it is entirely impotent.
Wealth, in this novel, does not protect the vulnerable. It weaponises them.
I would not wholly resist that reading, though I think Daniel overstates the determinism.
Because Dickens is equally interested in showing us that integrity resists the corrupting power of wealth — and that old Harmon himself knew it.
There is a remarkable passage in which the narrator describes the old man's relationship to Boffin and his wife.

"While he raged at them and reviled them for opposing him with the speech of the honest and true, it had scratched his stony heart, and he had perceived the powerlessness of all his wealth to buy them if he had addressed himself to the attempt."
'Scratched his stony heart' — what a phrase that is.
Not softened. Not broken. Merely scratched. Dickens is precise about the limits of what goodness can achieve in proximity to corruption.
And yet the Boffins' names are written down in the will. Their virtue has a consequence. That is not nothing.
That phrase — 'the powerlessness of all his wealth to buy them' — is also a legal statement, in a sense.
Testamentary power in Victorian England was absolute within certain limits. A man could disinherit anyone, reward anyone, humiliate anyone from beyond the grave.
What Dickens understands is that the will is the ultimate instrument of posthumous control — the dead man's grip on the living.
The Boffins are named because they cannot be bought. But they are still named — still brought within the machinery of the inheritance.
And that inheritance, as we see throughout the novel, contaminates everything it touches — even the honest and true.
Which brings us to John Harmon himself — and to the question of what it costs a person to grow up inside that machinery.
His own account of his return to England is one of the most psychologically dense passages Dickens ever wrote.
Listen to the accumulation of mistrusts here — and I want to read it because the rhythm itself is the argument.

"I came back, shrinking from my father's money, shrinking from my father's memory, mistrustful of being forced on a mercenary wife, mistrustful of my father's intention in thrusting that marriage on me, mistrustful that I was already growing avaricious."
Five iterations of mistrust, folding back on each other. The man cannot find solid ground anywhere — not in wealth, not in relationships, not even in his own character.
That is what a childhood of systematic cruelty produces — not poverty of means but poverty of selfhood.
Daniel has identified something real there — though I would name it differently.
What Dickens is tracing is not a political condition but a spiritual one — the progressive erosion of the capacity for trust.
And the deception Harmon adopts — taking the name Rokesmith, watching the Boffins from the shadows — is born of that erosion.
The narrator is quite explicit about the origin of this.

"When in the distrust engendered by his wretched childhood and the action for evil — never yet for good within his knowledge then — of his father and his father's wealth on all within their influence, he conceived the idea of his first deception, it was meant to be harmless."
'Never yet for good within his knowledge then.' That parenthesis is devastating.
The boy has grown to manhood without ever witnessing his father's wealth used for anything other than harm.
That is the moral catastrophe at the centre of this novel — not a class catastrophe, but a human one.
I think Edmund and Daniel are both right, and that is precisely what makes Dickens uncomfortable for any single interpretive framework.
Harmon's dilemma, as the narrator spells it out, is structurally insoluble.
If he comes back to life and accepts the inheritance, he must buy Bella. If he comes back to life and rejects it, he punishes her.
The law of testamentary succession has created a situation in which a man cannot behave honourably in any direction.
Deception is not Harmon's moral failure — it is the only space the system has left him to inhabit.
And while all of this is unfolding — this tragedy of identity and inheritance — Boffin, newly wealthy, is receiving the charity circulars.
I want to flag this passage because it is easy to read as pure comic relief — and it is not.
Boffin says — and the indignation here is entirely genuine, I think —

"Patrons and Patronesses, and Vice-Patrons and Vice-Patronesses, and Deceased Patrons and Deceased Patronesses, and Ex-Vice-Patrons and Ex-Vice-Patronesses, what does it all mean in the books of the Charities that come pouring in on Rokesmith as he sits among 'em pretty well up to his neck!"
The machinery of Victorian philanthropy is revealed as a system of social credit — a market in prestige conducted at the expense of the poor.
Five shillings makes you a Patron. The poor receive nothing but the honor of being patronised.
Boffin sees through it instantly — which is why his subsequent performance of miserliness is so painful to watch.
That is a striking place to pause — the honest man surrounded by the paperwork of false charity, the orphan in disguise sorting through it.
What Dickens has constructed is a world in which every institution — the family, the will, philanthropy itself — is a kind of trap.
We'll take that thread further in our next segment — looking at how specific characters find, or fail to find, a way to live honestly inside those traps.
Stay with us.
We've spent this episode tracing the lines that run through Our Mutual Friend — wealth, waste, identity, the river.
Now, as we close, I want each of our guests to take stock — not just of what Dickens shows us, but what endures.
Edmund, let's begin with you — you've been drawn throughout to the question of character, of individual moral weight.
Thank you. What strikes me, returning to the novel as a whole, is that Dickens earns his endings.
And he earns them because he has been so pitilessly honest about the forces arrayed against goodness.
Consider how the novel opens — with that magnificent portrait of poor Twemlow.
'Being first cousin to Lord Snigsworth, he was in frequent requisition, and at many houses might be said to represent the dining-table in its normal state.'
A human being reduced, with the most devastating courtesy, to a piece of furniture.
That is the society Dickens has assembled — one that classifies persons by their social utility.
And yet the novel's great argument is that some few souls — Bella, Eugene, Lizzie — resist that classification and become themselves.
That is not a political thesis. That is the oldest story there is.
I'll grant Edmund his ending, up to a point — because the novel's journey to that ending is brutal, and we shouldn't sentimentalise the cost.
Lizzie's words about the child surrounded by drunken people — that is where the novel's real weight sits.
'This poor ailing little creature has come to be what she is, surrounded by drunken people from her cradle — if she ever had one, Charley.'
That parenthesis — if she ever had one — is devastating. It's not pathos. It's an indictment.
Dickens is saying that for children born into that world, the very basics of human infancy cannot be assumed.
And that structural reality does not dissolve because Bella Wilfer finds love in a counting-house.
The two things coexist in this novel — and that tension is precisely what makes it great.
I think Daniel is quite right to hold those two registers together.
But I want to press on what transformation actually looks like when Dickens renders it in full.
The scene in the counting-house — when Rokesmith declares himself — is pure, unguarded feeling.
'My dear, dear girl; my gallant, generous, disinterested, courageous, noble girl!'
And then — Bella's response — she lifted her head and laid it on his breast, as if that were her head's chosen and lasting resting-place.
Now, one might call that sentimental. I call it earned.
Bella has paid an immense internal price — she has renounced the very mercenary instinct the novel began by diagnosing in her.
What I keep returning to, listening to both of you, is the novel's final image of the cost of violence — of what the system does to men who cannot escape it.
That passage where Bradley pursues Eugene toward the river — the landscape itself seems to anticipate what is coming.
'And then the red had the appearance of fading out of it and mounting up to Heaven, as we say that blood, guiltily shed, does.'
That phrase — guiltily shed — is doing extraordinary work.
Because whose guilt does Dickens mean? Bradley's, certainly — but also a society that has manufactured a man like Bradley, ground him into obsession, and then left him nowhere to go.
The river in this novel is not merely scenic. It is where the system deposits its human wreckage.
James has put his finger on exactly what I would call the novel's structural honesty.
Dickens cannot quite bring himself to a revolutionary conclusion — the happy endings are real and I don't deny them.
But the darkness he has placed on either side of those endings does not yield.
The child without a cradle, the blood mounting to heaven — those images remain in the room long after the novel is closed.
And I think that is precisely what great fiction does — it refuses to let the reader settle.
I find myself, rather against expectation, in agreement with Daniel on the lasting power of those images.
Our Mutual Friend is not a comfortable novel. It is a magnificent one.
And the measure of its greatness is precisely that it will not allow us to separate the joy of its endings from the weight of everything that precedes them.
A magnificent note on which to end — and I think a fair summation of what this novel demands of its readers.
Our Mutual Friend asks us to hold transformation and tragedy together, to honour the redemptions without forgetting the wreckage.
My thanks to Sir Edmund Leigh, Professor James Blackstone, and Dr Daniel Rosen for a conversation that has done justice to one of the great novels of the nineteenth century.
From all of us on Our Mutual Friend Unpacked — thank you for listening.

‘I dare say my birds sing better than other birds, and my flowers smell
      better than other flowers. For when I was a little child,’ in a tone as
      though it were ages ago, ‘the children that I used to see early in the
      morning were very different from any others that I ever saw. They were not
      like me; they were not chilled, anxious, ragged, or beaten; they were
      never in pain. They were not like the children of the neighbours; they
      never made me tremble all over, by setting up shrill noises, and they
      never mocked me. Such numbers of them too! All in white dresses, and with
      something shining on the borders, and on their heads, that I have never
      been able to imitate with my work, though I know it so well. They used to
      come down in long bright slanting rows, and say all together, “Who is this
      in pain! Who is this in pain!” When I told them who it was, they answered,
      “Come and play with us!” When I said “I never play! I can’t play!” they
      swept about me and took me up, and made me light. Then it was all
      delicious ease and rest till they laid me down, and said, all together,
      “Have patience, and we will come again.” Whenever they came back, I used
      to know they were coming before I saw the long bright rows, by hearing
      them ask, all together a long way off, “Who is this in pain! Who is this
      in pain!” And I used to cry out, “O my blessed children, it’s poor me.
      Have pity on me. Take me up and make me light!”’
c19:p76.summary: Jenny recounts a memory or vision from her childhood of celestial children in white who appeared to her, asking 'Who is this in pain?' and offering her comfort and rest. They promised to return, and their refrain became her solace.

The haggard head floated up the dark staircase, and softly descended
      nearer to the floor outside the outer door of the chambers. The doors of
      the rooms within, appeared to be standing open. There were rays of
      candlelight from one of them, and there was the sound of a footstep going
      about. There were two voices. The words they uttered were not
      distinguishable, but they were both the voices of men. In a few moments
      the voices were silent, and there was no sound of footstep, and the inner

      awake, staring and listening in the darkness outside the door as he spoke
      of it, he might have been less disposed to sleep, through the remainder of
      the night.

After hearing two male voices and candlelight, the voices cease and the light goes out. An omniscient narrator warns that had Lightwood seen Bradley's face watching from the darkness, he would have been even more disturbed.

      under the influence of the firelight, as if he were computing how many

‘It was only after a downward slide through something like a tube, and
      then a great noise and a sparkling and crackling as of fires, that the
      consciousness came upon me, “This is John Harmon drowning! John Harmon,
      struggle for your life. John Harmon, call on Heaven and save yourself!” I

‘Perfectly so, believe me; and with every sentiment of affectionate
      deference towards M. R. F. But if he amuses me, I can’t help it. When my
      eldest brother was born, of course the rest of us knew (I mean the rest of
      us would have known, if we had been in existence) that he was heir to the
      Family Embarrassments—we call it before the company the Family
      Estate. But when my second brother was going to be born by-and-by, “this,”
       says M. R. F., “is a little pillar of the church.”  Was  born, and became a
      pillar of the church; a very shaky one. My third brother appeared,
      considerably in advance of his engagement to my mother; but M. R. F., not
      at all put out by surprise, instantly declared him a Circumnavigator. Was
      pitch-forked into the Navy, but has not circumnavigated. I announced
      myself and was disposed of with the highly satisfactory results embodied
      before you. When my younger brother was half an hour old, it was settled
      by M. R. F. that he should have a mechanical genius. And so on. Therefore
      I say that M. R. F. amuses me.’
c12:p25.summary: Eugene recounts how his father pre-arranged careers for all his siblings (eldest as heir, second as clergyman, third as naval officer, himself as barrister and married man, youngest as mechanical genius), all with varying degrees of failure.
c12:p25.best_quote: When my second brother was going to be born by-and-by, "this," says M. R. F., "is a little pillar of the church." Was born, and became a pillar of the church; a very shaky one.

‘I have checked the calculation often, and it must have been two nights
      that I lay recovering in that public-house. Let me see. Yes. I am sure it
      was while I lay in that bed there, that the thought entered my head of
      turning the danger I had passed through, to the account of being for some
      time supposed to have disappeared mysteriously, and of proving Bella. The
      dread of our being forced on one another, and perpetuating the fate that
      seemed to have fallen on my father’s riches—the fate that they
      should lead to nothing but evil—was strong upon the moral timidity
      that dates from my childhood with my poor sister.
c30:p22.summary: While recovering in the public-house, John Harmon decides to let himself remain dead for a time to prove Bella's character and avoid perpetuating his father's wealth's curse.
c30:p22.best_quote: the thought entered my head of turning the danger I had passed through, to the account of being for some time supposed to have disappeared mysteriously, and of proving Bella

‘However, a sociable word or two on these mistakes became an easy
      introduction between us, and the weather was hot, and he helped me to a
      cool cabin on deck alongside his own, and his first school had been at
      Brussels as mine had been, and he had learnt French as I had learnt it,
      and he had a little history of himself to relate—God only knows how
      much of it true, and how much of it false—that had its likeness to
      mine. I had been a seaman too. So we got to be confidential together, and
      the more easily yet, because he and every one on board had known by
      general rumour what I was making the voyage to England for. By such
      degrees and means, he came to the knowledge of my uneasiness of mind, and

      some judgment of my allotted wife, before she could possibly know me for
      myself; also to try Mrs Boffin and give her a glad surprise. So the plot

Then, they all stood around the bed, and Mr Milvey, opening his book,
      began the service; so rarely associated with the shadow of death; so
      inseparable in the mind from a flush of life and gaiety and hope and
      health and joy. Bella thought how different from her own sunny little
      wedding, and wept. Mrs Milvey overflowed with pity, and wept too. The
      dolls’ dressmaker, with her hands before her face, wept in her golden
      bower. Reading in a low clear voice, and bending over Eugene, who kept his
      eyes upon him, Mr Milvey did his office with suitable simplicity. As the
      bridegroom could not move his hand, they touched his fingers with the
      ring, and so put it on the bride. When the two plighted their troth, she
      laid her hand on his and kept it there. When the ceremony was done, and
      all the rest departed from the room, she drew her arm under his head, and
      laid her own head down upon the pillow by his side.
c61:p96.summary: The marriage service is conducted; all stand around Eugene's bed as Mr Milvey reads the ceremony in low, clear tones; since Eugene cannot move his hand, the ring is placed on his fingers; Lizzie pledges her troth with her hand upon his; after the ceremony, she lies beside him with her head on his pillow.
